notes: Appeal by case stated on section 172 RTA 1988 and Article 6; outcome and authorities explicit.

enrichment.short_title: Section 172 driver identification and Article 6 for speeding offences
key_facts: The appellant was the registered keeper of a vehicle detected on three occasions by automatic cameras for speeding or failing to stop at a red light.
He received section 172 notices but refused to identify the driver on each occasion and was convicted of the section 172(2)(a) offence.
Before the Crown Court he argued that section 172(2) infringed his Article 6 fair trial rights by requiring self-incrimination.
The case was stated for the High Court on whether the Crown Court erred in ruling that he had a case to answer.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from the Crown Court to the Administrative Court.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the use of section 172(2) for speeding and red-light offences was held a proportionate legislative response to road safety.
enrichment.ratio: Compulsory driver identification under section 172(2) of the Road Traffic Act 1988 is a proportionate response to maintaining road safety even for regulatory offences such as speeding and failing to stop at a red light, and is consistent with Article 6 as explained in Brown v Stott and DPP v Wilson.
legal_issues: Whether section 172(2) infringes Article 6 by requiring a keeper to identify the driver
Whether compulsory identification is a disproportionate response for non-serious traffic offences
Whether Brown v Stott applies to speeding and traffic-light offences

notes: Interlocutory share-sale warranty appeal; Schedule 9 counsel opinion construction fully reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: Counsel opinion certificate for retention sum warranty claim
key_facts: Interleasing bought shares in Concept Automotive Services Ltd from Nicholas Morris under an agreement with a £4.5 million retention sum.
Schedule 9 required a counsel opinion of at least ten years' call before a warranty claim could withhold retention as a 'Good Claim'.
Counsel opined that a NAV warranty claim relating to overstated goodwill of the N&M Business had a reasonable chance of success, leading to retention of £3,369,000.
Morris challenged the opinion on interlocutory applications for disclosure, an implied term, and compliance with paragraph 10.4; Lightman J ruled for the buyer and Morris appealed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory appeal with permission from an order of Lightman J on applications relating to a pending warranty claim and counterclaim for release of the retention sum.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed with costs; the counsel opinion was held a binding contractual certificate if it met paragraph 10.4 on its face.
enrichment.ratio: Under Schedule 9 paragraph 10.4 of the share sale agreement, a counsel opinion operates as a contractual filter or certificate: provided it on its face states the required matters, the seller cannot go behind it to challenge the instructions or factual basis before trial, and no implied term requiring opinions to be based on true facts and proper instructions should be read into the agreement.
legal_issues: Whether an implied term required counsel's opinion to be based on true facts and proper instructions
Whether privilege over instructions was waived by supplying the opinion
Whether the opinion sufficiently stated bona fides, reasonable prospect of success, and quantum
Whether the pleaded claim was the same claim vouched in the opinion

enrichment.short_title: Mandamus to state case after excess alcohol conviction
key_facts: Eric Robertson was convicted of driving with excess alcohol after a collision and positive breath tests at Wandsworth police station on 5 August 2001.
He sought seven questions to be stated but the district judge refused as frivolous, holding the urine-sample procedure and breath evidence were sufficient.
He applied for judicial review of the refusal to state a case.
Fresh issues included admissibility of his admission that he was driving, timing of urine specimens under sections 7 and 8, and expert evidence that the breathalyser device had been altered.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a magistrates' court refusal under section 111(5) of the Magistrates' Courts Act 1980 to state a case after conviction for driving with excess alcohol.
enrichment.outcome: Judicial review allowed in part; mandatory order requiring the district judge to state a case on four specified questions, with disqualification suspended and costs from central funds.
enrichment.ratio: A refusal to state a case is Wednesbury reviewable and is frivolous only if no reasonable magistrate could regard the application as futile, misconceived, hopeless, or academic; here arguable points arose on section 172 admissibility, the urine-specimen timetable under sections 7 and 8, and whether reasons were required to reject uncontradicted expert evidence on device approval.

When the one-hour period for urine specimens begins under sections 7(5) and 8(2)

Whether the district judge needed reasons to reject expert evidence that the breathalyser was not an approved device

enrichment.short_title: Refusal to vary section 106 electrical retail floorspace cap
key_facts: Grantchester Retail Parks operated an out-of-centre retail park at Dallow Road, Luton subject to a 1993 section 106 agreement limiting electrical retail floorspace to 15,000 square feet.
It applied under section 106A to increase the limit, eventually seeking 35,000 square feet, but refused a council-proposed further restriction on non-bulky non-food retail.
Luton Borough Council refused the applications and the Secretary of State's inspector dismissed consolidated appeals in July 2002.
The claimant challenged the inspector's decision under section 288 on five grounds including failure to consider officer reports, sequential test logic, and town-centre impact reasoning.

enrichment.outcome: Application rejected; all five grounds of challenge failed and the inspector's decision was upheld.
enrichment.ratio: On a section 106A appeal the inspector lawfully exercised a planning judgment on whether a planning obligation continued to serve a useful purpose; failure to cite every officer report or a colleague inspector's decision does not invalidate the decision if relevant material was before the inspector and sequential-test and vitality-and-viability conclusions were adequately reasoned.

notes: Arbitration Act jurisdiction and construction of community arbitration agreement; partial success on representation.

enrichment.short_title: Arbitration Act appeal jurisdiction and Sikh community arbitration
key_facts: Two solicitor brothers, Davinder Singh Virdee and Amritpal Singh Virdi, agreed in 1998 to arbitrate their disputes before a Sikh community tribunal.
An earlier arbitral award was set aside by consent and the county court reconstituted the tribunal under section 18, resolving disputed procedural terms.
Virdee appealed limited permission granted by Mance LJ on arbitrator qualifications, legal representation, costs, and section 69 exclusion.
The respondent did not appear at the hearing though notified.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from HHJ Hallgarten QC's directions on reconstituting an arbitral tribunal and interpreting a community arbitration agreement.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part: no jurisdiction over arbitrator appointment under section 18(5); order varied to exclude unilateral legal representation and related costs declarations; permission to appeal on section 69 exclusion refused.
enrichment.ratio: Decisions under section 18(5) of the Arbitration Act 1996 on appointing or reconstituting an arbitral tribunal are final unless the judge grants permission to appeal; where the Act does not expressly bar appeal, the court may hear appeals on procedural directions such as legal representation, and the brothers' agreement impliedly excluded parties from instructing lawyers from the outset though the tribunal could permit legal argument on specific issues.
legal_issues: Whether the Court of Appeal had jurisdiction to hear an appeal from section 18 appointment directions
Whether arbitrators had to be members of the Sikh community under section 19
Whether the agreement excluded legal representation under section 36
Whether each party was to bear own costs under section 61(1)
Whether section 69 appeals on questions of law were excluded

notes: VAT rent-a-chair hairdressing appeal allowed; contract construction central to ratio.

enrichment.short_title: VAT supply by self-employed salon stylists under rent-a-chair
key_facts: Kieran Mullin Ltd operated eight ladies' hairdressing salons using identical written Rent a Chair contracts with self-employed stylists.
Customs and Excise assessed KML for VAT on full customer receipts, treating stylists as supplying services to the salon rather than directly to customers.
The VAT Tribunal held two stylists supplied customers directly but the other 43 stylists supplied KML; KML appealed.
KML retained customer receipts, paid stylists the balance after chair rent and service charges, and invoiced stylists for VAT on those charges.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the High Court on a point of law from a VAT and Duties Tribunal decision under section 11 of the Tribunals and Inquiries Act 1992.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the Tribunal decision was reversed and Customs and Excise's April 1999 direction requiring VAT on customer receipts was set aside.
enrichment.ratio: For VAT purposes the critical question is the contractual relationship between salon and stylist: under KML's Rent a Chair agreements the stylists rented chairs and supplied hairdressing services directly to customers, so customer payments were not consideration for supplies made by KML; salon control over attendance, holidays, and standards did not convert the arrangement into a services-to-the-salon structure.
legal_issues: Whether self-employed stylists under Rent a Chair contracts supplied hairdressing services to customers or to KML
Whether the Tribunal applied the wrong legal tests by focusing on control rather than contractual structure
Whether the Tribunal could distinguish between stylists on the same contract terms
Whether departure from National Hairdressing Federation VAT guidelines was fatal

notes: Millennium Commission grant refusal; reasons and misdirection grounds rejected.

enrichment.short_title: Adequacy of reasons for Millennium Commission grant refusal
key_facts: The Asha Foundation sought a £10 million capital grant from the Millennium Commission for a multicultural immigration and faith museum.
Asha had previously received and lost a conditional £10 million grant before applying successfully on eligibility but unsuccessfully on merit in the fifth funding round.
Twelve eligible applicants competed for about £19 million; the Commission's June 2001 letter said Asha's application was less attractive than others.
Asha challenged the refusal by judicial review for inadequate reasons and alleged misdirection.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from Lightman J's dismissal of an application for judicial review of the Millennium Commission's refusal of a fifth-round capital grant.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed with costs; leave to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Where a grant-making body has promised reasons and must choose between eligible competing applications, fairness requires appropriate reasons but not detailed comparative analysis of every commissioner’s views; stating that other eligible applications were preferred is sufficient for a discretionary comparative allocation such as the Millennium Commission's fifth round.
legal_issues: Whether the Commission gave adequate reasons for refusing Asha's grant application
Whether a promise in the application pack required fuller reasons than were given
Whether the Commission misdirected itself in applying appraisal criteria

notes: Large TCC adjudication nullity judgment; declarations and Insolvency Act point explicit at end.

enrichment.short_title: Nullity of construction adjudication applying wrong subcontract

statutes_considered.title: Housing Grants, Construction and Regeneration Act 1996

key_facts: Joinery Plus Ltd, in administration, performed DOM/2 subcontract joinery works for Laing at the Stakis London Metropole Hotel and a separate JCT subcontract at the Old Admiralty Building.
Joinery referred payment disputes to adjudication under the statutory Scheme; adjudicator Mr Hough awarded about £58,107 plus interest and VAT.
The decision erroneously applied Old Admiralty/JCT contractual material to the Stakis referral; the adjudicator acknowledged drafting errors but was not asked to correct them.
Laing paid £70,424.80; Joinery later sought Part 8 declarations that the decision was a nullity and that a fresh adjudication could be commenced.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Part 8 claim in the Technology and Construction Court for declarations as to the validity of a construction adjudication decision after the claimant entered administration.
enrichment.outcome: Declarations granted that the 6 August 2001 adjudication decision was a nullity, Joinery could commence a fresh adjudication, banking the cheque did not approbate the decision, and Laing's section 11(3)(d) Insolvency Act application to recover the payment was refused.
enrichment.ratio: An adjudicator who answers the referral by applying the wrong subcontract and wrong contractual documentation acts without jurisdiction, rendering the entire decision a nullity that cannot be cured by the court speculating on the outcome under the correct contract; accepting payment on account of general contractual entitlement does not approbate an invalid adjudication decision.
legal_issues: Whether the adjudicator's decision was valid despite referencing the wrong subcontract
Whether fundamental jurisdictional error made the whole decision a nullity
Whether Joinery approbated the decision by banking Laing's payment
Whether Joinery could refer the same disputes to a second adjudication
Whether Laing could recover the payment from an company in administration under section 11(3)(d)
